utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Lukic, you are ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For some reason, Mr. Lukic, you have eluded the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that. Once again, good morning, Your Honours. I'm not sure if everybody can hear me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, you are loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're ready to start our Defence case, at the outset of which I will be giving an opening statement as announced at the Pre-trial Conference. Your Honours, when, before the beginning of this trial, we were taking the decision as to whether we would be giving our opening statement at the beginning of the trial or whether we should do it now, before the start of our Defence case, we were aware of the fact that this moment will be a lot closer to the end than to the beginning of this trial. We were aware of the fact that we would be much closer to the closing arguments and that we should refrain from evaluating the massive amounts of evidence that has already been presented. On the other hand, we believe that we would be much better able to articulate what we believe to be the very purpose of giving an opening statement, the purpose being to announce to the Chamber what we would be presenting during our defence case and to focus on the most important allegations that will be heard. Our conclusion was we would be better able to achieve this once the Trial Chamber has already been acquainted with all the important evidence up to this point. We didn't think at the time, given the pre-trial brief and the list of the witnesses announced by the OTP, that there will be quite a turnaround in the OTP's presentation of evidence and that what I will call key witnesses would be dropped that were announced during the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief and opening statement. It is for this reason that, from our present standpoint, when nearly all the cards are on the table, we believe all the more that it is appropriate to give our opening statement now, before the beginning of our defence case. Your Honours, most of the cards are already on the table and have been laid on the table by all the parties. You are piecing together a mosaic of terrifying story. I am convinced that, after all the evidence so far, this image is still unclear and you are still lacking a lot of material information about key moments from the time covered by the indictment. When I met Mr. Sljivancanin - and we first met here in the Detention Unit - and when we first went through the indictment, as it was at the time, I informed him that the onus of proving those allocations was on the OTP and I informed him about the legal standards applied in presenting evidence before this Tribunal. He then told me that he wanted the truth to be established before this Tribunal. It was not his idea to defend himself from the allegations raised by the OTP. All he wanted was for the truth to be established about Ovcara, and this is what he told you in his own opening address. This was also the principle that we tried to abide by when preparing for this trial. After the end of the OTP case, we found ourselves facing a list of witnesses that we were intending to call. One thing I can tell you is that during our preparation, we talked to a great number of persons. Mr. Sljivancanin set another demand in relation to the witnesses that we would be calling. He said he would not be calling anyone to testify against their will but rather only those witnesses who were willing to appear before the Tribunal and testify. He said he did not want a single witness on his behalf asking for any form of protective measures or to testify in closed session. He was also adamant that he should appear as the first witness in his own defence case. We were lucky in terms of this position he took in regards the witnesses. Everyone we spoke to agreed to testify. There was one person who asked not to be called as a witness for family reasons and we simply didn't put his name on the list. There was another witness who has a serious health condition. We are still considering whether his possible testimony might adversely affect his health. All the remaining witnesses will be appearing in our defence case, according to a schedule that we have been trying to establish. In the presentation of our evidence, the Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin intends to call 16 viva voce witnesses, fact witnesses; two 92 bis witnesses already approved by the Trial Chamber, and their statements have been submitted. Our military and security expert will also be appearing live in this courtroom, since Mr. Moore has pointed out his wish to cross-examine him. Before anyone else, you will be hearing Mr. Sljivancanin taking the stand. We have also prepared to present and tender into evidence a certain number of written documents throughout our case. Your Honours, I will not use this time to describe the factual allegations as we see them. I will try to use this opening statement in order to guide you through important segments of our evidence that our witnesses will be testifying to. I wish to use this opportunity to draw your attention to some of the key moments of our evidence, events only partially elucidated, not elucidated at all, or even, let me say, intentionally obscured. I think the position of Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence is entirely clear to you. It was even at the pre-trial stage, the agreed fact stage, our cross-examination of OTP witnesses and other Defence witnesses, and our confronting the other witnesses about our own allegations and the facts as we see them. You know - and I'm only trying to point out what is most important about the sequence of events and allegations in the indictment - that our client, on the 19th of November, 1991, was escorting Mr. Vance, that he was in the Vukovar Hospital on that afternoon; that, on the 20th of November, he was again in the hospital; that he was not in the barracks on that day and that he was not at Ovcara on that day. This is the factual framework of our defence case. It may not have been until late in the proceedings that it became clear to you, Your Honours, why this Defence was so adamant to get the timing right described by various witnesses. It was the OTP that foisted this task on us. It was the OTP, through their own witnesses, whom they so extensively examined about Mr. Sljivancanin, who wanted to paint a picture of the events showing Mr. Sljivancanin being literally all over the place all the time, or to put it more simply, in different places at the same time. His face was a familiar one to all and sundry. The footage with Mr. Borsinger must have been shown a thousand times. All the photographs, all the TV footage, there wasn't a single witness who was not able to provide an accurate description of Sljivancanin's physical appearance. All those descriptions, precise descriptions of the physical appearance of Mr. Sljivancanin that the OTP were so insistent about became an important tool for our cross-examination. That is why, as early as the pre-trial brief, we said that it was through the OTP witnesses that we would really be getting our defence case underway, especially as to where Mr. Sljivancanin was or was not physically present. One thing I would like to clarify is that, throughout this trial so far, we have presented important evidence to corroborate our own position. We weren't merely biding our time, waiting for Mr. Sljivancanin to take the stand himself. What are the cards that we shall be laying on the table? What is it that you are about to hear during our defence case, Your Honours? I will now explain several things that I deem to be particularly important. You will hear testimony about the structure, the make-up of the Guards Brigade, its peculiar nature, its elite nature, as Mr. Moore called it. But this make-up and this structure will be explained in terms of what the facts were at the time, what the unit was trained for and what it was facing. You will hear about its peacetime activities and how it came to be involved in something that wasn't its original purpose, as well as the consequences of this exceptional use. Unequivocal evidence will be presented about the security organs and the security service in the JNA as a whole, especially in the Guards Brigade. We shall be paring back down to the bare bones the evidence to show you what they were doing, what they could possibly have done and what they could never have done based on the regulations or in purely factual terms. Obscuring the exact role of the security organs is the weapon used by all those who are jeopardised by their precise position and by their -- by any legal steps that they take. You will have in this courtroom witnesses have security organs from the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade of the 1st Military District and from the security administration. In addition to what happened in Vukovar, they will provide a lot of answers about the functioning of the security organ. Specifically, precise evidence shall be presented before you on the place and role of the military police in the Guards Brigade. The most competent people from the military police itself will take the stand; namely, the commanders of the 1st and 2nd Battalions of the military police, who were members of the command of the Operations Group South; the commander of the anti-terrorist company; and other commanding staff from the military police. They will present specific testimony on the events on the 19th and 20th, and what the OTP's particularly interested in - and I believe this Trial Chamber as well - about the relationship of the military police and the security organs de jure and de facto. On this subject, evidence shall be led by presenting the expert report of our expert, military security expert. We shall lead evidence on the arrival of the brigade itself in Vukovar, with focus primarily being on security problems. And you shall also have occasion to hear some details about the other activities of the Guards Brigade; the heroic moves of its members, the deaths of young soldiers and courageous commanding officers. We cannot be indifferent when only terrible things that have been presented by witnesses of the OTP are heard by this Court. We, therefore, consider that it is necessary for the facts to be comprehensively presented, primarily with a view in order to receive all the work done by the security organs during the fighting in Vukovar. But this is also substantial from the position of the Defence to the effect that the events and operations in Vukovar were neither apart nor in themselves a widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population. This was an armed conflict, a cruel one, with all the implications that fighting in the city entails, plus with elements of a civil war. But it was not an attack targeting the civilian population. You will hear evidence as to how the members of the Guards Brigade, how Veselin Sljivancanin and other commanding officers, did everything they could in order to help the civilian population of Vukovar and to alleviate the plight that had befallen them. Evidence will also be led about the problems in the OG South itself, on problems with the commanding officers, on the PT company, the leaving of the reserve members and the opposition of Sljivancanin to such a decision, the problems with volunteers and problems with TO members. We shall be presenting evidence on how and why and when Dusan Jaksic was replaced as commander and who appointed Miroljub Vujovic to head the TO. You will see that neither formally, nor factually, did Sljivancanin have any power to do that, although some have attributed that ability to him. The three charge days, so to speak, the 18th, the 19th and the 20th of November, 1991, will be the ones to which most of the evidence will be devoted. Virtually no witness of the OTP failed to contend -- to make a statement about Mr. Sljivancanin. We shall now have an opportunity to state our views on all such contentions and to confirm them if they are truthful or to challenge them if they are false. It is not our aim, Your Honours, to show that the OTP's witnesses are not convincing enough, but to provide, on our part, cogent evidence with a view to helping establish the truth. Evidence will be led before you on the surrender of the Mitnica detachment on the 18th of November, 1991, on Mr. Sljivancanin's activities in connection with his contacts with Marin Vidic, his encounter with the European Mission observers, among whom with witnesses Kypr and Schou, their escorting to tour Vukovar by Mr. Sljivancanin. You will hear evidence on how a group of captured people from Mitnica were taken to Ovcara on the 18th of November and how they were handed over. You will hear that from testimonies of the direct participants in that event. Important evidence shall also be led on events that evening at Ovcara, not only in the hangar but also at civilians of which testimony has been led in the proceedings so far. You will hear firsthand evidence of Mr. Vance and his visit to Vukovar on this event to which the OTP has devoted significant attention. You will have occasion to hear a witness say, "I decided that Mr. Vance should not visit the hospital." The witness who was the leader of this whole delegation on the behalf of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence will personally describe for you what happened during that visit which was fully covered, I shall stress, by the media. You will hear another officer of the JNA who, on that afternoon, was a member of the delegation of the JNA in negotiations with the European observers, what was the subject of the talks, and who attended the talks. You will also hear the witnesses of -- the testimony of eyewitnesses to events in the hospital on the 19th of November, 1991, the arrival of the security or military police, the arrival of Sljivancanin, his meeting with Vesna Bosonac and Vidic and what they told him on that occasion and how they behaved. Evidence shall be led before you on the arrival of a group of the security organs from the security administration and the 1st Military District on the 19th of November, 1991, to Negoslavci, the events in Velepromet that evening. On the other hand, you will hear about all the activities that Sljivancanin had that evening with Vesna Bosonac and Vidic, how General Vasiljevic arrived and what he did there when he came with his deputy Mr. Tuman [phoen]. Your Honours, you will have occasion to hear what happened on the 20th of November in the hospital. You will hear facts about the screening itself, the searching and the accommodation and the taking away of people from witnesses who were actively involved in all this. We shall show that the notes of Mr. Kypr were completely correct, even though the OTP sought to provide evidence to the effect that the person indicated in his notes as Colonel Pavkovic was, in fact, Sljivancanin. We shall prove that there was a dialogue between Mr. Pavkovic and Borsinger prior to the so widely media-covered dialogue between Sljivancanin and Borsinger. Two moments in the further course of events, in the view of the Defence of Mr. Sljivancanin, will particularly be focused on in the presentation of our evidence, two events that so far remained deliberately neglected in these proceedings; namely, what happened in the barracks on the 20th, who was present there, how the buses were secured, how the buses left; and the second moment, the meeting of the government of the SAO Slavonia Baranja and Western Srem, in Velepromet, while the buses were still in the barracks. How and why the convoy was sent to Ovcara from Vukovar, what kind of dialogues took place at the government meeting, what conclusions were reached and what the consequences were. The Defence of Veselin Sljivancanin asserts and shall prove that that is the key moment in this drama; that it is that moment that changed the course of events, that that is what sidetracked this evacuation, or rather, made it deviate from the standards that were shown only two days before that during the Mitnica evacuation, the task that could have been carried out completely clearly and precisely. Mr. Moore devoted, in his opening remarks when we look at the transcript, all of 16 lines and one page to the meeting of the government of the SAO Krajina. He called one witness, one live witness, and gave up on bringing a few more witnesses who were participants in this meeting. And he announced that he would call these witnesses in his pre-trial brief. Afterwards, he was very actively opposed to admitting Goran Hadzic's interview in evidence. Our Defence will give its own contribution to establishing the facts related to that meeting. We're going to shed light on that meeting from a different angle, and this will be done by an important participant. He will be the one to describe where the buses were supposed to go from the barracks and how it came to be that they went in a different direction. We are going to prove that Sljivancanin was not in the barracks on the 20th of November, at a single point in time, when the buses were there. Your Honours, I would like you to pay particular attention to evidence about the barracks and the meeting of the government. We would like to proffer evidence that will show that Ovcara would not have happened had the convoy not changed its course; namely, had it gone to Sremska Mitrovica as it was supposed to rather than to Ovcara. You will hear testimony about what happened at Ovcara on the 20th of November. We are going to provide evidence that he, Sljivancanin, on that day, was not present at Ovcara just as almost all Prosecution witnesses testified - victims, Croats, those who, as Mr. Moore, would put it, have no interest in concealing facts related to Sljivancanin's presence at Ovcara on that day. The accusations brought against all three accused persons in this case are very serious. Sljivancanin is being charged with extremely grave crimes. The procedure before this Tribunal made it possible for the Prosecution to make general allegations in this case, all of those that are in the Statute, including a form that was challenged in the appeals proceedings in Stakic. You will recall that indirect co-perpetration. Such broad charges constituted an additional burden on the Defence, making it incumbent for the Defence to speculate as to where the Prosecution is charging our clients in terms of them having planned, instigated, ordered, or committed acts within a joint criminal enterprise or whether they aided and abetted this enterprise. In the same way, the Defence was made to establish standards and elements indispensable for proving the existence of command responsibility, in accordance with Article 7(3). The Defence shall provide evidence, although we are not the ones who have the burden of proof, that Sljivancanin did not have any knowledge or that he could have assumed that a plan would be made against non-Serbs as described in the indictment. Your Honours, it's already been a year now that evidence has been called before you in terms of what the Prosecutor has charged in the indictment. Allegations are made about an event that took place 15 years ago. We are all aware of the fact that although memories may pertain to a period that has to be remembered, nevertheless, memory does fade on the part of any witness and therefore cannot be a fully reliable source for your own conclusions on facts. We know how important a role written documents should play in that situation in terms of analysing evidence. This Defence, just like the Prosecution, tried to obtain documents that they consider relevant for establishing the full truth about Ovcara. We also asked the institutions that are in charge a countless number of times, as the Prosecution did, and we received the same answer, that there is no documentation referring to this and it was destroyed during the NATO intervention. We wish that we could have proffered many more documents because we believe that, after all these years, this could be truly valid evidence in these proceedings. In the period that is envisaged for the Defence case of Mr. Sljivancanin, we will come to the day of the 20th of November, 2006, when 15 years from the Ovcara events will be commemorated. I deeply believe that, before this Court, we can rely on the professional standards of all the participants who will appear in this courtroom on that day and that we will all bear in mind the 11 bis proceedings held before the Chamber and the conclusions that led to having this trial held in The Hague after all. At the end of my introductory statement, opening statement, I wish to say that in the days ahead of us, you will have the opportunity of hearing evidence that primarily has to do with the defence of Mr. Sljivancanin in terms of the charges brought against him. You will hear his story and you will learn his truth. He wishes to tell that truth to you and the public. Mr. Sljivancanin is going to take the witness stand and tell you what he knows, but he will not know the answers to some of the most important questions related to what happened in Ovcara, the most important ones, in my view. On the basis of what you have heard so far, and on the basis of what I expect you will hear until the end, I believe, Your Honours, that you will remain deprived of direct testimony about important matters. Some persons who could, perhaps, give answers to you are no longer among the living. Some are trying to flee from this witness stand. Others, perhaps, do not care to have the truth established. If that is of relevance to you, you will have to reach conclusions about this on the basis of indirect evidence. I believe that by carefully assessing the evidence that you have heard and that you are yet to hear you will nevertheless be able to reach conclusions not only in terms of excluding the responsibility of Mr. Sljivancanin for what the indictment charges him with but also in terms of the question how and why Ovcara happened. Your Honours, before we call our first witness, Mr. Sljivancanin, I wish to thank you for having granted the Sljivancanin Defence time for presenting our evidence as we had asked for. We shall do our best to take full advantage of this period very rationally, in the spirit of Article 21(4)(E) of the Statute. I sincerely hope that the rest of the participants in this proceedings shall make an effort to render a sufficient contribution to completing this evidence in accordance with your decision and ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to call Mr. Sljivancanin so that we start with the testimony. [The accused Sljivancanin takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read allowed the affirmation which is on the card shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go through this quickly, since your personal details are agreed on. Please tell us something that the Chamber might want to know and something that's not in your personal details, and I'm talking about your family situation, your family background.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I'm married. My wife is a clerk. She has a job. I have three children. One of my daughters is a graduate of the law faculty and the other of the medical faculty. My son is still at college and he is a professional athlete, too. I have a granddaughter, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, do you know about the interpretation problems we are facing here? I'm not sure if you have a transcript in front of you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We discussed this a great deal. We're both fast speakers, so every time I finish my question, please make a pause and try to slow down a little when speaking.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know you were born in Montenegro in 1953. I will now go quickly with you through your military career. First of all, tell us a couple of words about your training at an early age -- rather, your upbringing, at an early age. What was your family like?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I never used to say I was born in Montenegro. I would always say I was born in Yugoslavia because that was the state I loved above all, and I think during my lifetime this was the most beautiful country in the world, at least that's what it was like for me. I was brought up in the spirit of love for all people, especially those living in Yugoslavia, if that means anything. My family, both on my father's and my mother's side, were part of the partisan struggle in World War II. Both my mother and my father were partisan fighters in World War II and they were involved in fighting all those who wanted to subjugate my country. It was patriotism and love of all people that were the guiding ideas in the area where I grew up. No one hated anyone else. The important thing was to be a good human being; that's what my father always said. Everything else was not so important for one's life and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are leading questions, Your Honours, and I do know that, but I would like to use a couple of these now just to get us through this as quickly as possible, to go through Mr. Sljivancanin's military career. I have a copy -- I have copies of these documents to be distributed to all the parties for his entire testimony. The first thing is his personal file so everybody can follow in English. We'll have this brought up in our e-court system, but I think this may actually speed us up a little. The Chamber is already familiar with Exhibit 592.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, just say yes or no, please, so that we may go through this quickly. I'm talking about your military career, which is quite a long one, if I may put it that way. You completed secondary military school in 1972; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next was the military academy, and you completed that in 1976; isn't that right, too?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After which you went to the Command Staff School for Tactics of the Land Forces. That was when?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: In 1987 or 1988, I think, thereabouts. 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Flying colours; right? Any commendation or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I was ranked the first, the top of my class.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1998, you finished the college for All People's Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And your average -- your grade point average was 9.41?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I was at the top of the class.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is some small errors in the transcript, but I think the documents speak for themselves. Military academy completed in 1976?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: 1976. Yes, that's right, 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You became second lieutenant in 1976. You became a lieutenant in 1977.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: That's right, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Captain, 1980?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Captain first class, 1984?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's how long it took. I think that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A major in 1988?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Probably that's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You became an infantry lieutenant colonel on the 26th of November, 1991, but this only takes effect as of the 18th of November, 1991. When were you actually supposed to be awarded this rank of lieutenant colonel, officially speaking?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I remember it being on the 22nd of December, 1991, which is the JNA Day. And you've read the documents, so I was actually awarded the rank on the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 18, line 15, my question was "a major."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You became a colonel in 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Podgorica, that's right, on the 31st of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your personal file, we have the exact course of your military service. I would like to focus on a couple of important dates that I believe might be helpful for the Chamber in order to follow your evidence. The file says that you came to the Guards Brigade in 1976; do you remember that? Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I'll remember that for as long as I live. It was an ideal for everybody to come and work and live close to Comrade Tito. So it was based on my own personal desire and because I was selected that I came to the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were first a member of the Infantry Battalion, but on the 2nd of September, 1980, you became commander of the military police company. Not long after, you became commander of the Special Purpose Military Police Company. We shall be talking about the peculiar nature of the Guards Brigade later on, but first tell me if all of this is correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: While Comrade Tito was still alive, the Guards Brigade had two guards battalions - that's what they were called - and one officers battalion. They were only into security and protocol. After Tito's death in 1980, I left the Guards Battalion where I was dealing with security and protocol. The Guards Brigade itself was being reorganized and I became commander of the military police company. In 1982, I became commander of the Special Purpose Military Police Company, which was only made up of junior officers. That's what we called them at the time, NCOs. The peculiarity of this company consisted in the fact that, for the first time in the JNA, units were being established for anti-terrorist struggle or anti-terrorist operations. I was one of the first to draft a programme and plan for these units, and the first such unit was in the Guards Brigade. This company only dealt with training officers for anti-terrorist operations and securing the Josip Broz Tito Memorial Centre, as well as some other important buildings and features, important for the top-most leadership and political leaders at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were then deputy commander of the military police battalion. That was from 1986 onwards; correct? In 1988, you became commander of the 1st A Battalion of the military police. We'll discuss the make-up of these battalions later on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, you were assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training. That was in 1989; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: That's right, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then, on the 7th of September, 1990, you became assistant chief of the security organ; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I was with staff of the Guards Brigade and I was holding a high-ranking position. I was the chief for operations and training. When Veljko Kadijevic became the federal minister, they were looking for someone who would do the security job for the minister. I was offered the job and I started working with the security organs. It was a lower-ranking position, to be sure, a demotion, if you like. But I loved working with that man and that's why I decided just to go there and give it a go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You became chief of the security organ on the 12th of August, 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. That was in August 1991. It was then that I became Chief of Security of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you came to Vukovar at the period of time covered by this indictment, you held that rank; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You later became Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade. That was in September of 1992, and then you were transferred to Podgorica where you were first commander of the brigade there, as of September 1993, after which you became commander of the Podgorica Corps, and that was in 1994. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: That's not quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's hear it, then.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: It's true that in 1992 I became Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade, and it was in 1993 that I was transferred by the then Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic. The transfer was to Podgorica. I never asked for it, but that was the order that eventually came. I was never the commander of the Podgorica Corps. In 1996, late February 1996, I was sent back to Belgrade, to the military school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the error was on my part. You were the commander of the Motorised A Battalion -- Brigade in the Podgorica Corps, from 1994 onwards; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I was the commander of the 5th Motorised Brigade, a formation in Podgorica between 1993 and February 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, you were back in Belgrade. That was in 1996. You worked in the -- as a desk officer in the special training centre at the higher military school.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then you were the chief of an organ for staff affairs in that same centre; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. After I was into training, I was now appointed Chief of Staff-related affairs in the military school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Finally, on the 21st of April, 2002, you became assistant chief for operative and staff-related affairs in the sector for schools and training.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Let me give you a hand with that. After I was chief of general affairs, there was a transformation, as they called it, a reorganisation, of the army and the same thing applied to the General Staff, and I was appointed assistant chief in the schooling and training sector for operative personnel-related and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your personal file states at the very end that you were removed from this duty for which, by a decision of the President of Yugoslavia, you were awarded the rank of major. You were retired on the 15th of January, 2002; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your rank at the time was colonel; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Major general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, general major, that was my establishment rank at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said you were involved in some purely technical work when you speak about the anti-terrorist company. Can you tell us briefly whether, in the course of your career, you took part in any technical aspects of military work; if so, what exactly, and when?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: When I became commander of the military -- of the Special Purpose Military Police Company, I helped draft these programmes and plans for the training of anti-terrorist units in the JNA. I actually completed the first section. It was later that I started working with Colonel Djordje Petrovic from the security administration. We analysed and wrote several things about the instructions on the training and use of the military police. This is about training military police units and anti-terrorist units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was that, roughly speaking; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: This went on for about three or four years. It started in 1982 and went on until I went to the General Staff School for Tactics to receive further training there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now talk about your arrival at the Guards Brigade. You said that the Guards Brigade was peculiar in nature while Tito was still alive, but then it was transformed, it was changed over into something else. Please tell us briefly about any links between the security organs while Tito was still alive -- security administration, then and later, according to the regulations that applied then and also later when you assumed these positions?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Everybody in this courtroom has heard already a great many witnesses talking about the Guards Brigade. Of all the witnesses who have so far appeared, I perhaps should be proud of the fact that I was the only one to serve in the Guards Brigade while Josip Broz Tito was still alive. This was a special unit of the JNA. And yes, if you choose to call it an elite unit, well, I suppose it was an elite unit in terms of its patriotism, in terms of its dedication, in terms of the way it did its work, and in terms of its respect for Tito, who was Yugoslavia. The Guards Brigade was not an elite unit in terms of how it carried out combat operations or its level of training for combat operations. It was an elite unit for purposes of our presentation and protocol and for securing the important persons, buildings, and archives in the former Yugoslavia. I don't know much about how the security organs functioned while Tito was still alive, because that's one of the things you asked me. I was a low-ranking officer at the time. But I do know that the Guards Brigade was subordinated directly to the chef du cabinet of the then-President of Yugoslavia, Tito. After his death, the Guards Brigade was subordinated to the chef du cabinet of the Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence. It did not have any direct command or chain of command linking it to any other bodies in the JNA, such as armies, military districts, corps, that sort of thing. The Guards Brigade remained unchanged, but then it started securing buildings in which the then-Presidency of the SFRY was staying and working. It also provided security for the various persons from the General Staff, especially the Federal Secretary of the Chief of Staff. Each unit, and this includes the Guards Brigade, is -- any unit is never established just for peacetime purposes and this applied to the Guards Brigade, too. Its tasks also included wartime duties and uses. After Tito's death, the purpose of the Guards Brigade was to continue to secure buildings and command posts of the Supreme Command in wartime conditions. Therefore, the training of such units within the Guards Brigade was done with a view to the securing of command posts of VIPs, and within the plan of the training of such units, we devoted less attention to offensive actions, to defensive actions and similar, which is something that the other units of the army had to be trained for. I can say that if one looks at the weapons and the equipment of it, the Guards Brigade had light infantry weapons and did not have any units within its framework that could have strong firing power, such as artillery, armoured units and similar. It is true that before the departure for Vukovar, an armoured battalion came and was comprised within the brigade. It came from Kraljevo and it did have more military might.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall now move to the military police. How was the military police in the Guards Brigade specific and how was the Guards Brigade specifically in relation to other motorised brigades as far as the military police is concerned?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Generally speaking, in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, the largest establishment unit of the military police was a battalion, and the military police was established, organised, in keeping with a need to secure the command posts of certain commands of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. The establishment unit which was in the military district was the battalion of the military police in the Independent Brigade and the A Formation Brigade, as we called it, which covered a very important tactical axis. We had the units of company strength, and in some installations, perhaps, there were squads, such as, for instance, in the military police -- military academy, the military court, et cetera. The greatest problem was how to training the young soldiers for these units, how to group them in the different centres. The Guards Brigade, being specific in terms of its purpose, from 1980, started also to train soldiers for its own needs. Up to that time, we received the trained soldiers from other units when we asked for them. According to war establishment, the brigade only had one battalion of military police, but in peacetime, it had two battalions. The 2nd Battalion dealt with the training of young soldiers which were -- they were to complete -- took five months and 22 days. Then they would be assigned to the 1st Battalion which dealt primarily, exclusively, with the securing of facilities and persons escorting columns, convoys, traffic security, and the like. All the MP units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army which were part of the military districts of the brigades also had their territorial jurisdiction in peacetime. That territorial jurisdiction meant that members of the military police were to control law and order and the implementation of the decisions of the legal service of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army by members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army on the territory in question. Let me clarify: If a soldier took leave and went to his home town and created any problems in terms of discipline or any other, at that time, in charge of intervening, of apprehending such a soldier, would be members of the military police which had jurisdiction in the territory in question, which would be addressed by the police of the city in question. The Guards Brigade, relative to other units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, did not have any territorial jurisdiction. It handled exclusively -- it was exclusively in charge of securing, as I've been saying, facilities in which state, the top the leadership, the top political leadership, and the Federal Secretary and the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any other motorised brigade have a military police battalion comprised within them? You have told me but give me a precise answer. That is very important.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The biggest establishment unit of the military police could be a company, so that in no brigade there existed a battalion except in the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Heading the military police battalion was whom, and to whom was that person answerable? And I'm talking exclusively about the Guards Brigade now.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The military police battalion in the Guards Brigade was commanded by the commander of the military police, and the rules precisely and clearly defined that the commander of the battalion was subordinated to the commander of the unit in question, in this case, the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us how it came to be set up? And how was this anti-terrorist company specifically? I'm specifically interested also in their chain of command. To whom were they subordinated; from whom did they receive their orders?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The counter-terrorist, as I've said, some witnesses have said here there was an anti-terrorist squad within the military police battalion of the then Federal Secretariat of National Defence that was formed first, and then in 1980, when the Guards Brigade was reorganised, that battalion of the military police came to be comprised within the Guards Brigade and the SSNO, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. And in 1982, there was set up a platoon for anti-terrorist operations. That was the first time that such units were formed in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army to carry out tasks and obligations which the times may require, because there were different terrorist actions; there were hijackings of airplanes and ships. So we followed the worldwide trend and we wanted also to plan for any such contingencies and to have a unit intervene in any such situations. The specificity of all that was that that unit -- to that unit were elected the most capable non-commissioned officers from the entire Yugoslav Peoples' Army. Their ability was reflected in the moral and psychological, as well as physical fitness and ability. I was fortunate, perhaps, to be able to go to the various units and elect my non-commissioned officers. What I was looking for and what I did was measure their physical fitness and their ability, and I received data about their family, to see that their mental and physical state, their family status, from other organs. Among others, I selected one young and capable non-commissioned officer. He also took the stand here. His indication was POO1. And I was hurt, because when you asked him whether he knew me - and I was his company commander from 1982 to 1987 - he actually said no, he didn't remember me. He didn't know who I was. But okay, that it is -- everyone is entitled to speak his mind. Let me just say that the training of these units was conducted in such a way that a day of training could not start without there being at least three hours of physical exercise at the beginning. I did not carry out this training by starting from scratch, because people had some training in the military school, but rather I would be the first one to overcome an obstacle, and anyone who couldn't follow suit would not be able to form part of my unit. If would be better if that someone was better than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me something else: What is the Military Police Special Purpose Squad?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The Military Police Special Purpose Squad was set up upon the arrival -- upon the assumption of Branko Mamula or Veljko Kadijevic of the post of Federal Secretary, I'm not quite sure, but it consisted of the elite non-commissioned officers of this unit for anti-terrorist operations who exclusively dealt with important security issues for the Federal Secretary of the Chief of Staff. And at the time when I was the Chief of Security, they were subordinated directly to me, who was in charge of that service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the only group, shall I say, of commanding personnel or non-commissioned officers from the military police who were directly subordinated to the Chief of Security in view of the specificity of their task; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: That is the only group of such people, and that was done by a special order of the Federal Secretary for National Defence that they would pursue those tasks with a view to not having those people change on a daily basis and not to disrupt the work and the obligations of the other units who were to pursue their basic tasks. And they were the best-trained and the best-fit people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I shall ask you one question but the answer is probably clear, in view of the specificity that you described. Was this squad at the Vukovar theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: This squad was not at the Vukovar front, but a part of the commanding personnel did come when General Adzic came to visit the units in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a couple more questions to cover the structure of the Guards Brigade. Tell me about the security organ. Later, we shall go through the rules of service and its articles, but tell me about the security organ in the Guards Brigade. To whom was it subordinated in the chain of command and to whom, in terms of professional control and command, and about its instructions and tasks in general.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: All this was regulated by the rules and regulations, and I shall be saying nothing new in relation to what we have already heard. But, of course, people are entitled, as I said, to say what they like. The Chief of Security in the brigade, including the Guards Brigade, is subordinated to the commander of the brigade and he exclusively does work related to that unit and to that command. The specificity, however, of the Guards Brigade is that the Chief of Security could also do other work, perform other duties from within the ambit of security organs which were of relevance to the members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, i.e., other persons who came to the buildings which were secured by the Guards Brigade, such as top political and military leaders. The commanding personnel, the desk officers in the Guards Brigade, for security - and I had two assistants in my squad and five desk officers - were subordinated to the Chief of Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. And I did exclusively work for the Guards Brigade, nothing outside the brigade. And in terms of professional guidance, professional command, the application of the methods of work of security organs, orientation, guidance, and everything else, from the time I assumed the post of Chief of Security, I was the one who was, in terms of such professional command, associated to the Chief of Security in the cabinet of the Federal Secretary from whom I received my instructions, exchanged experiences and liaised in terms of all the reports, and I sent reports on security to the chief of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time which we are interested in, which is the autumn of 1991, who was the assistant for security in the cabinet of the Federal Secretary?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The Chief of Security in the cabinet of the Federal Secretary in 1991 was Lieutenant Colonel Dragoljub Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A correction, but I believe you have corrected this in your answer to be precise. In your previous answer, on page 31, lines 19 and 20, you said that you were in the professional command, that you were subordinated to the Chief of Security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary, i.e., the assistant for security of the chief of cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this security and command relationship, did you ever receive any orders from the security administration?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: All the orders that were issued by the security administration came from the chief of the security cabinet, as far as I was concerned. So through the chief of cabinet of the Federal Secretary, there were orders -- not orders, but documents with which day they required us to do something or to help the security administration in dealing with their operational tasks, and we complied with such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we take a break now because I want to move to a document, a specific document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. We will, I think in view of the circumstances, have a half-hour break, Mr. Lukic. We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sljivancanin, during the course of the break, I spoke to several interpreters. They all indicated to me that we're going to have a problem with the transcript if we both do not slow down. I kindly ask you: Pause after my question. Shorter and more concise sentences. It is in your interest more than anyone else's to have everything stated clearly. Please bear that in mind. So we will both assist the interpreters in this way. And in the meantime, we've managed to provide copies of documents for them, documents that we will be working with, and I hope that that will be helpful.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I do apologise to the interpreters and I will try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to speak from the point of theory and practice about the work of security organs and therefore we are going to analyse certain provisions of the rules of service of security organs in the armed forces. That is Exhibit 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the registry to display the B/C/S version on e-court for the other participants because the honourable Trial Chamber and the Prosecution have hard copies in English before them.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: May I, before we start with the rules. When I gave an answer earlier on, in terms of this professional guidance with the security organs, I would like to add something else to that, since this was discussed in great detail here. There was no dual chain of command in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, ever. I repeat that once again. Every Chief of Security is subordinated, with regard to all matters, to the commander of the unit that he is in, just like any other officer. I, as Chief of Security of the Guards Motorised Brigade, from this professional point of view, was guided exclusively with regard to tasks relating to counter-intelligence that had to do with state security affairs and that have to do with undermining and destroying the constitutional order of Yugoslavia as well as questions and tasks pertaining to intelligence work within the Guards Brigade and which would reduce their combat readiness and the moral political situation. These tasks could not have been public by nature. They were carried out according to certain methods and principles as regulated by the rules of security organs. All the rest was resolved at brigade level, just like for every other officer, and there are no unknowns involved in that. As Chief of Security or the security organ, I could not resolve any task or I could not go out to any assignment without the brigade commander knowing about that, and no officer from the security organs could do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us in a few words - and then we are going to deal with the articles themselves - what is the purview of the security organs' work? Are there different tasks involved there, and what kind, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I've already stated in my previous answer that security organs are professional organs of units, commands, and institutions that carry out tasks related to state security and that have to do with protection from undermining and destroying the constitutional order of the state, that is to say, the then Yugoslavia. Security organs had tasks that they carried out as the mainstays of those tasks, whereas they had other tasks that they took part in with other units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. Security organs were primarily protagonists of preventing intelligence activities vis-a-vis units and within units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army; then, discovering and preventing hostile activities within and vis-a-vis units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. They were also protagonists of counter-intelligence protection of documents, facilities, and personnages of importance to the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. They were also protagonists of collecting and verifying certain data that is important for the work of security organs with regard to certain persons from the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. It was their duty to develop an information network for analysing data within the security organs, and one of their tasks was to prepare security organs and train them for the eventuality of a war. As far as I know, those were the tasks whose protagonists the security organs were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Can we place on the screen and you can have a look at it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 6, that is, Exhibit 107, Your Honours. The B/C/S version is on page 6; the English version, page 7, Your Honours; 00920105.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is roughly what you said. What I see in Article 6 is what you referred to just now, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I have it before me and I see here on the screen, that is, the Rules of Service of Security Organs in the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and here in Article 6, it says, "Security organs are responsible for --" I don't think it's necessary for me to read all of this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, in addition to these tasks, there are other tasks that they participate in, the security organs participate in them, together with other units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you now. Let's not read through all of this. It is Article 7. We don't really want to read all of this, Mr. Sljivancanin. Could you just explain briefly what tasks these are, where security organs participate, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you already referred to security organs participating in, as stated in the Article 7, "the protection and prevention of serious crimes may involve ..." and so on and so forth. And then, "the recommendation, regulation and organisation of security and self-protection measures ..." and so on and so forth; I already said that. "... planning and programming of for permanent reserve members ..." et cetera, et cetera. Then "professional work in military police units..." Then "the units of the military police as such ..." And also in previously started criminal proceedings and possibly -- exposing the possibility of an aggression against the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you explain in your own words what the difference is, from an essential point of view, what is the difference between the words "mainstays," "protagonists" and the like, and, on the other hand, "participation"? So what does a security organ do when they are the mainstays of a certain activity and what do they do when they participate in a certain activity?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, when they are the mainstay, then they are the most important protagonist in that particular job. They spend most of their time working on those jobs, whereas for the rest, when necessary, they participate or take part if the need arises for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, what is stated in Article 6 and 7, does it actually constitute the purview of work of security organs?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: It is certainly quite clear there, because this is the way it's prescribed through the rules of service of security organs. There is really no comment for me to make because this is stated clearly in the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you to look at Article 16 and I'm going to ask you about who commands security organs. Who are they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Your Honours, it is page 10 in the English version; 00920108. And for e-court, it is page 9 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I've already explained that. The security organ is subordinated to the commander of the unit that he is in, and as for counter-intelligence, he receives professional guidance from the security organ of the Superior Command. As you said, it's all regulated here and stated in Article 16, in the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 18, can you comment on that. That is actually what you said just now, but can you tell me what it means, in your view? What does this management mean, from a professional point of view, in terms of security organs? We have not dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, in the same article, it is precisely stated that security organs of the Superior Command - in my case, it was the cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence - from a professional point of view, they are in charge of the security organs of the Guards Brigade, that is, the unit that I was in. And as I said, they only provide professional guidance to them in counter-intelligence work. I've already referred to particular questions in this regard: Preventing undermining the constitutional order of the country and preventing hostile activity from taking place in the Guards Brigade in this specific case, which would reduce its combat readiness and the level of morale for carrying out its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us be quite simple. The security organ of the Superior Command, in addition to providing this professional guidance, can it issue any orders in terms of the chain of command to the security organ of the subordinate unit?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The security organ from the Superior Command can only channel the security organ subordinated to it, if we can put it way, "subordinated." In terms of finding the best methods and applying the methods of security organs in terms of resolving a particular matter from the domain of counter-intelligence work, we cannot issue any tasks in terms of command. If there is a task where the security organ from the subordinate command should be engaged outside the purview of the unit that it is in, then the security organ has to address the commander of the unit in writing and to ask for this organ to be engaged in other work outside the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give me your comment on paragraph 3 of Article 19, because it is directly related to Article 17 - the Trial Chamber will interpret that - but these provisional or temporary groups and this assignment in terms of different tasks.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: In Article 19, paragraph 3, it is clearly stated that superior commands and institutions can send certain teams and security organs to carry out tasks in subordinate units but only within the purview of security. It can also be in the garrison and the territory, as stated here, or institutions that have to do with carrying out counter-intelligence tasks. Such officers have to receive authorisation and also written orders in order to carry out such an order. When they are to carry out this task, once they arrive in the unit, they, first and foremost, report to the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about an example that we heard about in this trial. Say a group from the security administration arrives in Vukovar on a certain mission. Are they subordinated to you, and do they take orders from you and from the command of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: It's superfluous for me to interpret this, but it's already in the rules, isn't it? As far as I remember - and we'll be talking about that later - a certain group of officers arrived, security officers from the security administration, a group of officers from the 1st Military District. They came to us from the superior commands. They could not be subordinated to us. They were carrying out only those assignments previously assigned to them by whoever had sent them there to begin with. But they couldn't come to our unit or to our area of control to carry out any missions whatsoever there, unless they had previously received a written order. Throughout the duration of that particular assignment or mission, they can channel the work of the security organ, of the unit, to which they came. They can provide guidelines on how best to accomplish their assignments, how best to accomplish -- to help them accomplish the assignments that they were there for.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now please analyse Article 23, the relationship between the security organs and the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is page 11, 00920109; the B/C/S page is 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've heard evidence here - and we're about to hear more evidence - by military police witnesses. What does this mean, where it says that the security organ provides technical or professional management for a military police unit? Can you please put that in more graphic terms for us.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: This issue is explained in the instruction on the application of the rules for the military police, in paragraph 14 of that set of rules, where there is a precise definition of how a security organ provides specialist or technical guidance for a military police unit. It's been a long time, but if I remember correctly, the issues boil down to this: The first thing is drafting programmes and plans for military police training; next, the control of how these programmes and plans are implemented and actually training the units; selection of personnel or of men, if you like, that will make up those military police units. Security organs are also involved in analyzing any tasks carried out by military police, and later they try to build on that experience to find other ways, the best ways, of going about such problems. Next, they are involved in monitoring and evaluating the combat-readiness of military police units alongside with other bodies belonging to the command of which that particular military police unit is a part. Next, they advise the unit commander and make proposals on how best to use a certain military police unit on a certain mission, and how to use it to the best possible effect. There may be other issues, but you can go back to paragraph 14. As far as I remember, those are the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's not do the exam routine and just keep listing all these minutia. Can a security organ issue any orders to a military police commander pursuant to any of the various regulations that you've analysed and listed? You were MP; you were also a security organ, so you have both perspectives, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: As far as that's concerned, for a security organ to be able to carry out its most material tasks, the ones that I've addressed, the security organ must always keep one thing in mind: It must avoid any form of command while issuing assignments and orders. A security organ must be a mother to everyone in a unit; the behaviour must be like that of a mother. There can be no command and the rules don't allow for that. If a security organ thinks that a military police unit should be used for a certain assignment, from the purview of the security organ, this security organ must first draw up a plan on what exactly they want to achieve, what sort of manpower should be involved, military police manpower, in this case. And then this is submitted to the commander for approval. If the plan is approved, then they can go ahead. They can take as many men as they need and use them to achieve a certain mission from the direct purview of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go for a moment to Article 48. The English pages are 19 and 20; the B/C/S is page 16 and that's in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We needn't read this out, not the entire paragraph, anyway. Let me ask you this: Can a security organ carry out any assignments? Does this rule, or any other rule, envisage the possibility for a security organ to carry out assignments outside its strictest purview, which we have just described?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I've heard a lot of evidence here - you've all heard a lot of evidence - where everybody's said whatever they liked, it seems. But one thing I would like to point out to the Chamber and everyone in this courtroom is that the JNA was a serious institution. Rules and prescriptions were complied with, and until they started breaking up our country, we remained throughout a strong and well-respected institution. Not just anyone could be appointed commander in the JNA. People were hand-picked, and the choice was normally based on individual ability and skills. Each commander was supposed to understand the work of all his underlings, all his subordinates, as well as the work of security organs. In some way, these were organs who performed work that was, well, if I might put it that way, secret. At least some of it was. A commander knew and the security organs knew that a security organ could carry out assignments outside their functional purview but only such tasks that were related to the security organ and no other tasks at all. Personally, as head of a security organ, I would never embark on a task unless it was something from within the purview of the usual work of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 57. Just a couple of questions about the security administration subject that was widely debated before this Chamber. There's a whole chapter in reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 57; the English page is 23 and the B/C/S reference is 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Article 57, second paragraph, can you please comment on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Security administration was an institution within the Secretariat for All People's Defence and it had great powers. I never worked in the security administration. All I can tell you is what you can read in the rule and what was well known. Their assignment was to provide technical and professional guidance to other security organs, even those outside the JNA, such as the TO, the Territorial Defence, which was a constituent part of the armed forces of the SFRY. And this applied to all security-related issues. There was a very important element in the work of security organs. This element entailed cooperation. And it was probably in terms of the territorial division of the units over the entire area of the SFRY that they formed networks. But I did not involve myself in any of these issues except as they were occurring in the Guards Brigade. So I wasn't involved in any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You sort of answered the question, but let's try to be specific. Could anyone from the security administration issue any orders to you in the command sense of the term?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: In the purely command sense, for anyone to issue any orders to me, they would have had to go through the brigade commander, and that was the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned something about the relationship between the security administration and the TO, and I believe this is something that everybody in the courtroom wants to know about. I think Article 58 addresses that issue. In case of an imminent danger of war or a state of emergency, they provide technical guidance for bodies belonging to the Territorial Defence. You, as part of OG South, while you worked as Chief of Security of the Guards Brigade, did you provide any technical or professional assistance in terms of the security of any TO units in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: You just mentioned OG South. My views of OG South are quite different from what we have heard so far. As for the Territorial Defence, and we'll probably be addressing this issue at a later stage, I was not in charge of providing any sort of guidance to them, nor did I ever provide any sort of guidance. Only they came to me, for example, to ask for help on something that had to do directly with a certain mission and the carrying out of this mission. Perhaps there were persons who were violating the rules and order prevailing in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, I must warn you, Mr. Sljivancanin: Please so down.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What relationship was there between the security organ in the command, the technical sense of the term, and temporary formations?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what I know. I can tell you about my experience on the ground. There is no technical control carried out by security organs in temporary units. The organ providing technical guidance to me as a security organ is the security organ of my Superior Command. And, again, this was the Chief of Security of the federal minister's cabinet. And I can show that based on a number of documents that we'll probably be using. The unit commanders, if they are involved in this temporarily - and this can be true for 15 or 16 or 17 days on a certain mission, for example - they're still in touch with their original command, and you've seen that. In this case, there are daily combat reports that were sent by the commander of the Guards Brigade to the 1st Military District to which they were subordinated for the time, but specifically for the mission of lifting the siege of the barracks in Vukovar. And they always sent daily reports to their original command, which was the federal minister's cabinet. So that was exactly the procedure applied in the work of security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small correction for the transcript. The answer is entirely all right, but my question, on page 45, lines 4 and 5: "What was the relationship in temporary formations?" And then you provided your answer. In the sense in which you have just provided this answer, if an operations group is a temporary formation, I believe that is one thing at least that we all agree on in this courtroom. In a purely technical sense, as a security organ, who was Mr. Drago Vukosavljevic subordinated to, or rather, the security organ of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade, for as long as they were part of OG South? Who would they be submitting their reports to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: If you analyse thoroughly all those issues, the issues that had to do with technical guidance, if you go back to the rules and look at the way these were defined there, then one thing is clear: When carrying out a combat mission, there is no training; there is no drafting plans and programmes for training; there is no checking combat-readiness; there is no personnel selection; there is nothing like that involved at that stage. The Chief of Security of the 80th Brigade was supposed to be submitting reports to his own superior and receive from him, in return, technical assistance and reports covering that. But for the more practical matters, he would have had to take up any issues with his own brigade commander. He could have - but this is something we will probably be discussing later - he could have warned the security organs of the Guards Brigade about some issues to do with counter-intelligence, something that he heard was occurring in our own unit. It would have been easier for us to track these things down then. Likewise, we could have warned him. I do have to say, however, that this security organ, as far as I remember, emerged for the first time once the mission had already been accomplished, the mission that we were in Vukovar for. There was, by this time, no need any longer for me to get in touch or provide any sort of guidance to them. The task was completed on the 18th. If you look at all the war logs and all the other documents, you can check when this unit, or any of its parts, arrived in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who, then, is the superior in terms of specialist direction to the security organ of the 80th Brigade?
