Also, during their stay in Vukovar, the superior organ, in terms of specialised -- specialist direction, according to the rules of service of the security organs, is the Chief of Security of the 80th Motorised Brigade -- was the organ of security of the corps of the 24th, one -- the formation from which they came --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: From Kragujevac, you mean? Well, I don't know right now from where they were. I heard and I read here that it was the 24th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we are going to move to a different topic all together. My next question has to do with facts. I believe that this Trial Chamber and all of us in the courtroom know that certain political senses and certain political changes started mounting and happening on an intensive case at the end of the '80s and beginning of the '90s. Can you tell us, Mr. Sljivancanin, how did these political developments, especially in 1990 and 1991, how were they reflected on you, on members of the JNA, on your specific unit and on you personally?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I believe that it was not only me, but every honourable and decent human being in the then state of Yugoslavia, in particular members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, it was humiliating to all of them and all of us and it was inconceivable for us that something like that should be happening in our state. I have always spoken publicly about those events and I am not ashamed of anything. That is why I am here, to speak publicly, because it was a shame, it was a disgrace, that young men of 18 or 19 years of age, who came to do their military service, and that was according to the law, that they should be killed, strangulated by members of their own people with whom we had lived until the day before that. And I believe that all of you have seen images of a soldier securing the command in Split without a single live bullet in his rifle, and that soldier was killed and was strangulated by some hooligans. I, as the security chief, Chief of Security, had occasion to read the letters which were written by commanding staff and soldiers to the Federal Secretary for National Defence and others have not had that unit. They wrote mostly from Slovenia, from Croatia. And I know that young men who came to study at the naval academy in Split were strangled and thrown into the sea; that they did not dare go out in the street and use the telephone to call their parents, or to the post office. I know that they were surrounded, encircled. Warehouses of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army were also surrounded, which warehouses were secured by squads, five to ten troops strong, and they would even be blown up. And there was torture and there was killing and so on and so forth. There is a lot to say - let me not go on - but it was very ugly and literally incredible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I have a short answer, please. This is also related to the political circumstances at the time. What was your position regarding the burgeoning of nationalism at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: When I said what the commanding staff and the soldiers were writing in their letters sent from the ten republics of the former Yugoslavia, Croatia and Slovenia, that does not mean that such occurrences did not also occur in Serbia. There were verbal attacks there also. We were being attacked as being members of the communist party, "the commies," they called us, and those were the verbal assaults. And, of course, there was nationalism also there and in some milieus where I worked. And any and every -- nationalism was, to me, something that had to be condemned and prevented at any price. And I especially have that attitude towards nationalism coming from the -- from the town where I hailed from and from my own environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard testimony before this Court - I believe that this was during the Prosecution case and also in regard to Mr. Mrksic - where we talked about the Spegelj affair and the engagement of certain commanding officers in that particular affair. I'm not interested in details but I am interested about it in terms of our analysis of the regulations. Could the security administration engage anyone from the Guards Brigade to perform any specific task?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Testimony has been given in that regard here already. The security administration, as I've already said in answering certain questions before, engaged part of the commanding staff from the Guards Brigade but solely by written order through the commander, i.e., through the cabinet of the Federal Secretary. And the following is true: The commander, for instance, I, myself, would not know at the specific moment what would be the task that we would be engaged on, but I did know that they would go to the security administration up to the accomplishment of that task, and no one had the right to actually inquire what would be his mission. The task would be handled by the commanding officer who would be in charge at that point of the operational processing, as we called it, in order to deal with certain questions, counter-intelligence tasks, in order to prevent intelligence and hostile work targeting units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army on the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. But I should like to stress once again: The commanding officers could not go to perform such a task without there having been received a written order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any instances of desertion in the brigade? When did that happen, and what did you do when it did?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: When we talked about the elite character of the Guards Brigade, namely, up until the 1990s, it was inconceivable that a soldier, let alone a commanding officer, in the Guards Brigade should be late from his leave or be late for work, half an hour or an hour, let alone desert. We never had any such occurrences. And let me underline, once again, that being a -- becoming a member of the Guards Brigade was also on a voluntary principle. It wasn't only by dint of law. So that desertion -- desertion occurred for the first time towards the late '80s, early '90s - I cannot remember the exact date - with, first, the Albanian soldiers, serving military service, starting to desert, and the greatest blow to me personally - and I believe all the other commanding personnel of the Guards Brigade - was when the troops of Slovene ethnicity deserted, which I believe was in the beginning of 1991. By operational work, we managed to reverse that desertion and bring them back to the unit. But immediately the following day, orders -- an order came from the Superior Command that the Slovenian troops should be sent to do their military service to the Republic of Slovenia. In my view, that already meant the start of the break-up of Yugoslavia, with an erosion also of the morals and combat-readiness of the units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army starting as well, because young people of other ethnicities as well, individuals, also started wondering why, if the Slovenians should be serving their military service in Slovenia, why wouldn't they be allowed to do the same in their own republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question regarding this particular topic of political developments. Did there start certain obstructions on the part of the military boards, the military department, when it came to the assigning of specific soldiers to the Guards Brigade; and if that was the case, what can you say about it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The security organs of the Guards Brigade kept analysing and checking the personnel that was assigned to the brigade, especially the troops, the soldiers, because we had to be mindful of the fact that it was not the same thing to assign a soldier and arm him with a rifle and ammunition and have him secure a foreign delegation or a top foreign political or military leader or a certain facility, because that person can do a lot with arms, the weapons, issued him. We cannot stand by his side at all times. And I remember well that when I was analysing the soldiers' composition in 1991 and when I informed the commander of the brigade of my results, the worst soldiers were actually sent to do their military service in the Guards Brigade. The overwhelming majority of the soldiers had bad characteristics, as, for instance, children of divorced parents, drop-outs from schools; they engaged in some petty crimes; were mentally unstable or not sufficiently stable. In a nutshell - and this is something that I only realised later - the chiefs of the military districts of the military departments that assigned such soldiers to us, to serve in our brigade, actually did that deliberately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not pursue these preliminary stories any longer, although there would be a lot more to say from your career in securing different political leaders and the different encounters of high political leaders, between the political leaders of the former Yugoslavia as the country was breaking up. Now I shall move to Vukovar. When did the brigade set out for Vukovar? With what mission? And how and when did it arrive in Vukovar? And please speak a bit more slowly, Mr. Sljivancanin. If you can, follow the transcript and adjust your pace to it, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: In order not to repeat myself - and this is something that we already know - the Guards Brigade was assigned to the mission of lifting the blockade on the Vukovar barracks and the creation of normal conditions for the work and life of all citizens of the city of Vukovar, and disarming all paramilitary units in that city. It set out on that task on the 30th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you set out, what happened en route? Did anything happen en route? And where were you quartered? What was your final destination?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, normally, as for any other task, the commander of the brigade issued instructions/tasks to the subordinate commanders. I actually did not dwell much on those issues. The brigade marched, according to the rules and the regulations which were then in force in the -- governing the conduct of the units of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, they marched up to the town of Sid, up to which place it went unhindered. From Sid, through Tovarnik and Oriolik, up to Negoslavci, there were frequent attacks on the column of our brigade. Personally, I was hit. Actually, the vehicle that I was in was targeted near the village of Djeletovci. My late driver, Popovic, when the first shell impacted on the road in front of the tires of our vehicle, he cried out, "Comrade Major, let us stop." I saw a small elevation on the road in front of us and I told him, "No. What do you mean, 'Stop'? Step on it so that we can seek shelter behind that hill." So that we avoided being hit, because two shells actually landed and we avoided being hit in the beginning. The units deployed for battle. There were -- some were wounded. There were no killed. And I realised at that point that those units were actually following the slogan that we saw in the video footage on Spegelj that we had seen, our former general, our former General Spegelj, who up -- brought me and educated me, which was: First target the commanding officers and we will then easily deal with the troops who will disperse once you have hit the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Let me just add this: Once we arrived in the area of Negoslavci, mortar fire was opened at the units of the brigade. And I remember well that a soldier who was at the headquarters of the Guards Brigade - and the headquarters was actually the unit which directly catered to the command to create the necessary conditions for the quartering/overnight stays, and so on - when they started erecting the first tents in a garden for overnight stays, this soldier was a Croat, and a mortar shell landed and killed him on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A brief question and a brief reply. Where was the seat of the department of security, the squad of security, of the Guards Brigade during the Vukovar operation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: During the execution of the tasks in Vukovar, the command of the brigade deployed its basic combat post in the village of Negoslavci and the logistics rear command post in the village of Berak. Security organs were deployed in the region of the basic command post in the house in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who of your commanding staff of the squad of the security organs stayed -- was with you on this mission, who stayed in Belgrade, and who did what of the commanding personnel? I mean the names that have been mentioned before the Court and will be material for later proceedings.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Two officers from the security organs remained in Belgrade to carry out this task, and along with me, the following persons went to Vukovar for security organs -- sometime after the 5th of October, I got yet another security organ from the security administration who was appointed my assistant for counter-intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us their names and ranks and what they covered in terms of their work? What work were they actually engaged in?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I went to Vukovar to carry out this task as Chief of Security. My then assistant for military police affairs, Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic, and at the same time he covered the 1st and 2nd Battalion of the military police from a security point of view. Then, Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic set out as well, who covered, from a security point of view, the 2nd Motorised Battalion and at the same time, Assault Detachment 2 in Vukovar. Then, Captain Borce Karanfilov set out as well. In peacetime, he covered the 1st Motorised Battalion from a security point of view; however, since one of my security organs could not perform due to certain problems, I gave Karanfilov the rear command post and the rear units at that command post from the point of view of security. Then, Desk Officer Momcilovic set out, too, who was involved in control services at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who came later, and what did that officer do?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: At that time in the security organ of the Guards Brigade, there was only one trained officer, Captain Karanfilov had completed a course for security officers. I, Major Vukasinovic and Srecko Borisavljevic came to the security organs - how should I put it - on the eve of the Vukovar operation when we had not completed the course yet. And I asked instructions from the cabinet of the Chief of Staff of the Federal Secretary for National Defence. And we had Mladen Karan assigned to us; he was captain first class at that time. He had done security with security organs work, and he was appointed my assistant for counter-intelligence. He came to Vukovar, if I am not mistaken, and I hope that I remember this correctly, it was after the 6th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there officers in charge of security who were attached to motorised battalions as well? And what kind of persons were they? And how were they attached to your squad?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: In terms of war formation, in terms of peacetime establishment, every motorised battalion of the Guards Brigade had a security officer from the reserve force, and these officers were mobilised. Now, I remember with certainty that an officer named Stanisic was mobilised and came to the battalion. He worked as a security officer in the battalion and he was only subordinated to the commander of the battalion. He contacted me with regard to counter-intelligence protection, and he resolved all other matters at battalion level. As for the other units -- I mean, while in the battalions of the military police, there weren't any security officers in terms of the war establishment, whereas in the 2nd Battalion I think that this officer did not actually come; he did not respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, can we hear now what the primary, basic, tasks were that your squad dealt with during the Vukovar operation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, the primary tasks that our squad dealt with during the Vukovar operation were primarily those that I already referred to, that are based on the rules of service. However, now, on the ground, they became expanded. It consisted of the following: That at that time, due to propaganda and everything that was going on vis-a-vis the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, conditions had to be created for all delegations coming to the zone where combat actions were taking place in terms of deblocking barracks and disarming paramilitaries, and all accredited journalists who we were told would be coming in, we were supposed to provide security for them and not to conceal anything from them. They should be allowed to see everything. That was the position I took as well; however, nothing should happen to them either. What surprised me at the time, and what affected me as Chief of Security, was that on the first day, we lost ten soldiers when we came to Vukovar and we didn't know where they were. This was on the 2nd of October, 1991, when they went to help their comrades in the barracks and they simply went missing then. I, as Chief of Security and as a human being, who looked upon all these soldiers in the Guards Brigade and all others as my own children, the most important task for me was to find these soldiers and to save their lives. That is why all the time, from the first instant, I was at the very front line. I didn't have to be there all the time, but I was there all the time in order to find out where those soldiers were and what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you first reach the barracks in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: At my own initiative, if I can put it that way, I know I reported to the commander and I tried to get to the Vukovar barracks immediately either on the 30th, when we arrived, or on the morning of the next day. And I suffered grave consequences, if I can put it that way. I was attacked by mortar shells, and it was very hard for me to get through; I even had to leave my vehicle behind. However, I had to spend two or three hours sitting in the basement of a house and then I actually waited for a lull in the fighting. And then I met a lieutenant colonel there whose name was Rajko Novakovic. Indeed, I experienced something that I could not have dreamed of happening; namely, that people lived in such conditions as our soldiers did at that time in the barracks. But I also experienced something else: That these young men did not want to leave the barracks at the cost of their lives, that they didn't want to get out, although we were suggesting to them to get out and to come and join our brigade. When I returned, I told the commander about this and, of course, after that an action was planned to deblock the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps somebody else is going to talk about that. Just tell us, after how many days was the barracks deblocked; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, the action for deblocking the barracks started in the morning hours of the 2nd of October. I remember that on that day, I came to Dalmatinska Street, which is the first time I came across one of the radio transmitters that was used at that time by the members of the ZNG, of the Croat forces, and we came across a machine-gun nest there that was near that street. And they probably abandoned their positions there once our units arrived. From that moment onwards, I kept listening to their conversations through that radio transmitter, and I was trying to find out who was controlling who and what.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You, as security organ, why did you find this radio transmitter that you came across to be important?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: It was most important for me so that, through their coded names, I could find out the strength and disposition of their forces. I often used this radio transmitter to talk to some of my former colleagues who crossed over to the other side, the paramilitary forces of Croatia, and I found out that they had been officers of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. And I was trying to persuade them that we should not fight; that only until yesterday we had lived together and lived well; and let us leave it to the politicians to see what the sociopolitical system of Yugoslavia is going to be like; and that we should not kill each other; and that we should not destroy that kind of beautiful city, the way Vukovar was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Sljivancanin, I would like to ask you to draw something for us, to mark something on a map that is relevant to me and, I believe, to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registry please place map 156, Exhibit 156, on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know the procedure, Mr. Sljivancanin. You will be assisted by the usher; you will get a pen. The first thing that I would like you to mark, if you can, on this map - and during our preparation for your testimony you said that this suited you fine - is to show what the area of responsibility of Operations Group South was.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The zone of responsibility of Operations Group South, as we've heard here from the experts who spoke about it, has a certain boundary, or rather, certain boundaries on all sides. This is where the zone was. This is the right-hand boundary of the zone. There it is. The village of Berak cannot be seen where the rear command post was in terms of depth. So the boundary was the village of Sotin and then further on, Grabovo. You cannot see it because of the picture. And then further on towards the village of Berak. To the left, feature 102 on the road leading from Bogdanovci to Vukovar. Then the village of Petrovci and further on towards Berak. In terms of depth, the Vuka River and its mouth into the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this zone 1, so to speak, could you mark the zone of responsibility of Operations Group South. What units were next to you, JNA units, that took part in this operation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Operations Group South kept changing its composition. At first and all the time, the Guards Motorised Brigade was there. Then, for a while, perhaps for five or six days, the 453rd Brigade from Sremska Mitrovica was there and then it was withdrawn from the area, I think, on the 5th or 6th of October. Then, there was the Podunavska Brigade, the Danubian Brigade, which also, in the month of October, got out of Operations Group South. And the 20th Partisan Brigade of the Territorial Defence came, which got out of the composition of the -- on the 18th of November, as far as I managed to see here in the war log, and it came to replace this 20th Partisan Brigade, or rather, the 80th Motorised Brigade came to replace the 20th Partisan Brigade in the following way: On the day when this task was being accomplished, that is to say, on the 18th of November, 1991, Operations Group South, while we cannot call it that, although it was not that way, according to the rules, the Motorised Guards Brigade came there. The 80th Motorised Brigade and a Territorial Defence detachment of Vukovar, which acted in concert with the Guards Brigade, and the Territorial Defence detachment of Kragujevac which acted in concert with the Guards Brigade in its area of responsibility. Then there was the Territorial Defence detachment of Sremska Mitrovica which was resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade. And there was the so-called tactical group of the 195th Motorised Brigade which was resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade. And there was the 544th Armoured Battalion that was resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have an intervention in terms of the transcript. Page 60, line 7, the witness said, from the Vuka River to the Danube River, when he was drawing this boundary in depth of the Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Vuka River to the mouth into the Danube.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was on the other side of the Vuka? Whose area of responsibility was that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: On the other side of the Vuka River, as far as I know, were the units of the 12th Corps of the 1st Military District. They established some groups within their composition, but I was not there and I do not know what they called these groups. But I know it was the 12th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were they mentioned as Operations Group North?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Over here I heard in these testimonies, and in various documents that were presented here, that somebody was calling them Operations Group North and somebody else was calling them Tactical Group North. Now, what their actual name was is hard for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you place number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Number 2 where this --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where the Novi Sad Corps is?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Novi Sad Corps, number 2. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the boundary is the river Vuka?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The river Vuka and further on. I don't know what their boundaries are. But the task, in terms of how far our unit was supposed to go, was to the Vuka River, and the Novi Sad Corps, from the north up to the Vuka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please before we have this document removed, or rather, admitted into evidence, can we see the position of the guards division on this map.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Units of the 1st Guards Division were the left-hand neighbour of the Guards Motorised Brigade, meaning the village of Petrovci, the village of Marinci, and then on to Nustar and Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Put a number 3 there, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I request that this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 815, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if we could please have this same map but an unmarked one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, if you can, please mark on this map the area of responsibility of the Guards Brigade and that of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade within OG South, respectively. We want to know about the 18th, 19th and 20th, of course.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1991, the Guards Motorised Brigade, which was working on this mission with, as far as I remember, the Vukovar TO detachment, and the Kragujevac TO detachment had an area that was within the area covered by OG South. In terms of the area's depth, the boundary would be the Vuka River, where it bordered on the corps, and to the left, elevation 102, excluding the village of Petrovci and then on to the village of Berak. On the right, it included the village of Mitnica, or rather, the neighbourhood of Mitnica, and then past Negoslavci and on to the village of Berak. This was the area covered by the Guards Motorised Brigade within OG South, and it worked with the units that were in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Put a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: All right. The 80th Motorised Brigade, with units resubordinated to it by orders of the commander of the Operations Group - again, I repeat this is the Sremska Mitrovica TO detachment, the 544th Armoured Battalion, and the tactical group that came from the 195th Motorised Brigade - their area was -- the left-hand border of their area was the same as the Guards Brigade Mitnica and next to the village of Negoslavci, and on the right, not including the village of Sotin but past it, and then the area next to Grabovo, facing the village of Berak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the area to the right of the Guards Motorised Brigade, number 2; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: This was the situation on the 18th of November, 1991, to the best of my recollection, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd request that this be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With Exhibit Number 816, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a third time, the same map, but could we please blow up the Negoslavci area as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this helpful, Mr. Sljivancanin? You know what I wanted to show now. Do you like this map?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, it's fine, if you want me to draw the position of the command post in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. Our next topic: Where, in your opinion, was the command of the Guards Brigade of Operations Group South? Can you please draw that for us first and please put a number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The command post of the brigade, at this point in time we're talking about the Guards Brigade, is an area about one and a half kilometres by one and a half kilometres. And in that area, you have all the other elements of the command - the operations room, the commander's place, the signals room, the security organ, whatever the commander says -- whoever the commander says should be there. And then there was the command post which I said was deployed in Berak. In Negoslavci, the following were set up and in the following order, in solid buildings: In one of these buildings over here - I'll draw a circle there and I'll put a number 1 there - this was the commander's place and the operations room. Security organs. The security organ was right in this house, across the way from this church. Right here. I'll put a number 2 there. If you want to know about this, too, on the 9th of November, the commander issued an order to set up town commands. By this order, Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic was appointed town commander of the village of Negoslavci, and his place was right there in this house. I'll mark this with a small circle and put a number 3 there. In addition to this, something I knew: I often held meetings with international organisations in a house where there was the permanent press centre throughout the duration of combat operations in Vukovar. The house was right here. It was Captain Forca [as interpreted] who was in charge of this. Number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: What I knew at the time, as for the other elements, something else that I can tell you, because they were helping me to track down the perpetrators of any crimes: There were the forensic technicians from the military police battalion, and they worked closely together with my assistant for counter-intelligence. They were based in a building right here. I'll put a number 5 there. As for the rest --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No matter. No matter.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: As for the rest, the moral guidance organ was here, too, as well as the judge. Everybody else was stationed in the village of Berak, at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction: Page 65, line 10, Captain Zvorcan not Captain Forca. Can we please have this admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 817, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be a good idea to have the break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we continue, I would like to make an official correction in the transcript. When officers and their names were being mentioned belonging to the security organ, on page 55, we see that there are omissions in the text. But just to clarify matters for the benefit of the transcript, page 55, line 6, the witness said "Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic"; line 9, he said "Captain First Class Srecko Borisavljevic"; line 11, he said "Captain Borce Karanfilov"; and line 16, "Momcilovic"; and line 25, "Mladen Karan."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, now for something that occurred during the combat operations, which I believe to be of relevance to this trial. Did the military police unit join the fray, the combat operations in Vukovar; if so, when and why?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: A lot of evidence has been adduced, as well as documents, on the use of these units used to lift the siege of the barracks and disarm the paramilitary units. What I want to say is: Those documents are not orders. They're not orders; they're just commands and decisions of the commander on the use of forces to accomplish that mission at the time. Military orders are something entirely different. These decisions are often revised by the commander as a mission develops or fails to develop. At the outset there is the first decision of the commander of the Guards Brigade, and pursuant to this order, part of the military police units were attached to the motorised battalion, which, in practical terms and under the rules that were applied at the time, was simply not possible. As I pointed out already, the lowest-level unit, comprising a military police presence within its composition, is a brigade; however, since the Guards Brigade comprised quite a number of policemen, the commander had every right to make this decision. We analysed the decision here, and what it says is, at the outset of combat operations, the commander tasked one battalion minus a company to secure the command posts. He decided to use another battalion as a reserve and later used it to establish control over the territory. However, as the enemy was well-organised, strong and well-equipped, we were, in a way, surprised. We had not been trained for that, nor had we ever believed that we would find ourselves facing a situation where, in our own country, we would have to fight our own people, to put it that way. Personally, I was convinced at the time that it would be sufficient for us to just turn up as soldiers and that the entire population of the town, regardless of their ethnicity, would accept our presence as someone who was there to help everyone and restore order. However, that was not the case. Immediately, on day 1, we suffered great losses on account of this surprise factor, and the commander had to step in and do something about it. He used the anti-terrorist unit to strengthen the 2nd Assault Detachment, and to establish control over the area on along Sajmiste Street, at the junction between the 1st and the 2nd Assault Detachments, or rather, the 1st and the 2nd Motorised Battalions. Later on, as changes occurred and the reservists left the Guards Brigade, we were also taking measures to disarm all volunteers and those units who were not in line with the discipline. The 2nd Battalion of the military police was introduced and used along the front line where combat was underway with the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you, first of all, please tell us whether there were any problems with officers. First of all, quite specifically, the officers of the anti-terrorist company, were there any problems with those, or with the officers of the 2nd Battalion of the military police in relation to their active involvement in combat?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I'm able to depict the situation for you by just talking about it. We had emerged from peacetime conditions and our families were safe and there was no shooting. No state of war had been declared. It was never our intention to wage war on anybody at all. We were just there and we had certain missions. And I told you what these missions were. We had to preserve the lives of those young soldiers, return them to their parents. It was inconceivable for a country theoretically at peace to see all those young soldiers being killed, because the behaviour of an officer is different in peacetime conditions and, again, it's different under conditions of war, when there is the risk involved that soldiers might be killed. So this was the first such situation that we came across. The first signs of hesitation were in that anti-terrorist unit, and much to my surprise, the focus of all this was the commander of the 1st Battalion of the military police. This is something that I wrote down in my observations. I thought that this was one of the results of enemy activity in trying to disrupt or impair the combat morale of that particular unit. Just briefly, something I found out later on by intelligence activity: The commander of this anti-terrorist unit - and, after all, he confided in me and then told me about this - he had received a letter from his wife that, how should I put it, had an adverse effect on him and was causing him to feel mentally unstable. He was beginning to worry whether Yugoslavia would survive or not, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was Maric, Mladen Maric, right, the commander of the anti-terrorist unit? He was the very person I was going to ask you about. This person you're talking about is P0001, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Commander P0001, the commander of the anti-terrorist platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What became of Mladen Maric?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Mladen Maric, the commander of the anti-terrorist company, was seriously wounded when he tried to enter the barracks with his unit to supply some food and water to the soldiers in there. He was the first to get in. He wanted to get some food and water to the soldiers who had been inside the barracks for quite sometime. And then he was taken for treatment, to receive treatment, in Belgrade. It was towards the end of combat operations, towards the end of that particular mission that he was returned to Vukovar and rejoined his unit. But I can't remember the specific date when he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there, at any particular point in time, changes in the post of commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion, instead of the -- no, the post of the 2nd Military Police Battalion? I correct myself.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I can give you a reply right away. After the first day, when the units entered the barracks, the commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion complained to the commander of the brigade that he was not mentally fit to continue to be in command, that he needed assistance, and the commander assigned a commanding officer from the operations and training organ, a deputy commander, to assist this commander. And after the first failure by the first commander of the Military Police Battalion to discharge his task, he was transferred to the military medical academy, the military hospital, for treatment, and Captain First Class Jovan Susic, I believe, was appointed in his stead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As this will involve reports that we will later comment on, how was he sent from the 1st Battalion of the military police to Belgrade for treatment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion was Major Branislav Kavalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So Susic replaced him later.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. When he left, Susic replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Chief of the General Staff visit the Vukovar battlefield; and if he did, when was this, and what can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, Lieutenant General Blagoje Adzic, visited the units in the zone of what we call south on the 1st of November, and that is probably noted in the log of the Guards Brigade, in 1991. I remember that vividly also because the -- because the Chief of the General Staff came, that's one thing; and secondly, because I was exposed to criticism then. So General Adzic arrived at the commander's command post. The commander briefed him on the situation in the combat zone. The major problems that we were faced with were the order that had come from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia to the effect to the reserve forces should be returned, and I personally, and others, thought ourselves to be an armed force of the Socialist Federalist Republic of Yugoslavia and that as such we needed to be respected. But that's the way things were and that's what happened. And we had problems with other units, with other formations, which were not part of the Guards Brigade, and the resubordination of specific units; I particularly have in mind the Territorial Defence and volunteers. Thereafter, General Adzic expressed the desire to visit the young soldiers who were on the front line to see whether it was, indeed, combat fighting or something that we had not experienced before, as even before going to Vukovar, I was in charge of security for General Adzic. With the approval, with permission, from Mrksic, I proposed that the general should go and see the soldiers, and that I certainly can see to it that his security is guaranteed and that nothing would happen to him. And I proposed the plan, how we should proceed, that we should reduce security, because every movement of ours was watched and artillery fire was opened on all moving vehicles. The General accepted my suggestion and we set out, I and his three escorts from this special purpose department or squad, i.e., non-commissioned officers who were under my direct command. With General Adzic came the chef du cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence, Colonel Vuk Obradovic, and he asked to go with me. I took the general to exactly the front line, the barracks, Dalmatinska Street, the Vuteks stadium, where the anti-terrorist units were. And we came to the command of the 1st Assault Detachment to see Major Tesic. There, the general was received by Colonel Mrksic. From there, we toured a number of units from the 1st Assault Detachment, and I remember when they heard that General Adzic had arrived, that many civilians - women, elderly people - wanted to come out and greet the general and have their photos taken with him. I never asked any of the people whether they were Hungarians, Ruthenians, Croatians, Serbs. For me, to me, they were all equal, and to General Adzic as well. And we stayed in that disposition area of the 1st Assault Detachment for about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall not go into all the details. What I would like to hear from you, to wrap up this visit quickly and briefly, you said that you came under some criticism.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just finish this. General Adzic later came to the positions of the mortar company of the 1st Assault Detachment, 120-millimetre mortars, and that is where he ended his tour of the unit. I had to write a report on the visit and I was criticised for the first time by General Vasiljevic, who later came to inspect, and he told me that I was exposing myself to a grave danger; that I should not have allowed myself to take the general to the first line of fighting, and what the consequences would have been for us had he been wounded or killed or something else, and what a risk I had been running. Because he said it was not ordinary, under such circumstances, before checking all the security measures and verifying all such steps, for the Chief of the General Staff to be taken to precisely the front line, whereas I thought that at that particular time they were not armed conflicts, that it was fighting paramilitary formations and terrorist groups, and that the general had to see all the problems that our young soldiers were faced with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Vasiljevic suggest anything to you in respect of any further such visits in terms of your desirable behaviour and conduct vis-a-vis such persons?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He suggested, as an experienced and still-commanding officer, he suggested that I should never do anything of the kind again, especially not in respect of larger delegations or higher-level delegations and important persons; that, first, I would have to undertake an evaluation, a plan of the visit, and to take them and escort them exclusively to where it was safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the testimony of P018, Witness P018, who had personally escorted General Adzic. Do you have any comment on account of that? You were there, personally present.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was present and I heard the different testimonies here also. But this is a great nonsense. Not that I'm making things up or just telling stories for story's sake. But General Adzic had security, professionally trained people for that particular task, and there were a large number of MPs, military police, members there so that such a person could not even approach him, come close to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm interested in another episode which we shall also go through by consulting documents later. Who was Dusan Jaksic, and what do you know about his replacement? How did that come about, the appointment of Miroljub Vujevic to that post?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I know full well who Dusan Jaksic was, and I heard his testimony here as well. It is simply surprising to one, but then, again, one perhaps should not be all that surprised because I have seen that people can say whatever they please. Dusan Jaksic, when we arrived in Vukovar, was the commander of the Territorial Defence detachment of Vukovar. I know that initially he attended all the meetings held by the commander of the Operational Group, which he attended together with Major Borivoje Tesic. I know that I, too, was given information by Major Tesic, and in the informative talks, the interviews that we had, which is one of the methods of security organs' work, that Jaksic did not enjoy confidence in his own detachment; that he was not aware of the actual situation in his detachment; that there were instances of lack of discipline, breach of discipline; that he didn't know the strength of his detachment, the number of members; and that he was very often absent from the detachment and that no one knew where he went. Through the other security desk officers, the collected data, we also learned that he liaised with certain persons from that territory who were smugglers; that is not to say that he was involved in the smuggling. And the reference was made that I wrote something about it. I never wrote anything about him. You can see that by consulting all of my reports. Anyway, Jaksic came with Tesic to talk to Commander Mrksic very often and brief him on these problems, and he expressed the opinion, he, himself, expressed the opinion that he was unfit to command units at the front. Therefore, he proposed that he be replaced and that someone from his formation be installed in his stead, while the units were executing their combat tasks, until they had executed it. As far as I recall, that is the way it happened. Mrksic, according to the rules of the brigade, did not have the right at that time to replace and appoint the commander of the Territorial Defence, and I believe that he consulted his assistant in charge of manning and mobilisation, who was a professional in that regard and who gave him the guidelines to follow in the particular instance. I informed Mrksic about Borivoje Tesic's observations about Jaksic and, in agreement with Jaksic personally, Commander Mrksic and Tesic - so in agreement, all of them - decided, as far as I know, for Jaksic to remain in the Territorial Defence detachment to coordinate the rear operations, the supplies, et cetera, while the units on the front line executing the combat missions should be guided by Miroljub Vujevic, who was his commander of the 1st Territorial Defence Company at the time. That was the way it was until the task was completed. Later, I don't know whether anyone wrote an order on the relieving or dismissal or appointment of anyone, but I believe that even the layperson is certainly clear on the fact, as Jaksic said here -- and this is not to defend me. I just want to say: As the Chief of Security, I could not, I did not, have the powers, nor did I appoint or dismiss anyone from duty. So, for what it's worth, I did not get any operational processing report for Jaksic, and you can find nothing of the kind in my reports. And as far as what he said is concerned, that is perhaps some observation of his. Maybe he knows something more about it, but I don't. Maybe, as I said, he knows more about it himself and that's why he said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who is Boro Bugunovic, and what do you know about this man?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I know that allegedly at that time, Boro Bugunovic was a minister in a government of the -- what they called the autonomous district of Western Srem, which was self-proclaimed. They self-proclaimed it. I didn't believe in it and I didn't respect it. I did not honour it, because the state of Yugoslavia existed at the time. Yugoslav laws were in force. There existed the republics and there existed the municipalities. I had never heard of such governments prior to that time. But he introduced himself as a minister in that government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Of the interior, Minister of the Interior. By operational work, the collection of data, I received information that he was engaged in smuggling; in arms dealing, actually. I called Mr. Bugunovic for a talk, an informative talk, because he lived in Negoslavci and I knew where his house was, but he would not come. He did not want to come. So I informed the commander about this fact and he allowed me to send the military police to actually bring him in, to call him and bring him in for a talk. He came for a talk. We also searched his house and we found weapons in it. The weapons that he found is something that he, as a civilian, should not have had. I wrote a security report, a security memorandum, addressing it to the chief of cabinet for security of the Federal Secretary, and he responded and told me what further course of action I should take. At that informative talk, I asked Mr. Bugunovic to report on a daily basis to my security organ, security officer; however, he actually left the territory and I never, ever saw him again, until the end of the mission in Vukovar. Later, I found out that he had been in Novi Sad and in Sid, but as we left the territory, I didn't know anything about his whereabouts then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Soon we will analyse these documents, these reports of yours. Before we start doing that, could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you sent reports, how you sent them, to whom you sent these reports, and what kind of correspondence existed between you and other security organs. Did they send anything to you; if so, what?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I had two ways of reporting. Firstly, regular reports at command meetings. I reported to the commander about all observations related to security in the zone that was controlled by the Guards Motorised Brigade; namely, whenever these meetings were held and, if necessary, even on extra occasions if there was anything relevant of this nature or if the commander would call me in requesting some information. There was such information when, through professional lines, I got information regarding counter-intelligence. I would receive information in terms of counter-intelligence tasks to the Chief of Security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence. Later on, when General Aca Vasiljevic came to Vukovar, he asked that this information that I write to the Chief of Security and the cabinet of the Federal Secretary, that I should submit copies to the security administration so that less time would go by in terms of the reports that would come eventually to his office as well. So that is how I sent this information to this security administration as well. I sent this information in sometimes every day; sometimes every two days or every three days, depending on what was going on and depending on what I had to report about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from whom did you receive information and instructions in relation to security organs along the lines of this professional information, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: In terms of tasks for the unit and what was going on in the Guards Brigade, I heard about these tasks at the briefing with the commander. As for counter-intelligence, I only received information and tasks from the Chief of Security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence, which is what we will see through the documents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During combat actions, did you receive professional direction from the security organs of the 1st Army?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I never received any such document, nor did they cooperate with me with regard to any security matter. It was only with the representatives of the command in Sid with regard to lists and perpetrators of crimes who were brought in that we found while carrying out our tasks up until the 18th of November. That is the only cooperation I had with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why? What was in Sid at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Sid, there was some command, part of the command of the 1st Military District. That's where the security organ was. Or was it the security organ of the 1st Guards Division? I cannot say exactly now because did I not attend a single meeting with them but somebody was there. And this is where the reception centre was, outside the zone of combat actions, where persons who were suspected of having committed crimes were processed or persons who surrendered in the combat zone with weapons, up until the 18th of November. On the 18th, an order was issued, because there were a great many such people who cropped up and they should be taken to Sremska Mitrovica instead of Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was there in Sremska Mitrovica at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know now, and as far as I saw from these documents, this is where a camp was established for taking in perpetrators of criminal offences in the zone where combat action was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I would like to start this analysis. We are going to do this several times during this evidence, but we are going to analyse some of the 65 documents that we wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first documents that I would like to have a look at - I think that is the first document you also have on this list - that is a letter of the security administration dated the 3rd of October, 1991; 3D 050001 is the number of the document. It is marked as 3D 01 as a 65 ter document. I don't know if we can see it on e-court, on the screen. If we can have it enlarged please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, first of all, tell me, in terms of form, what is this that we see now on our screens and this copy that you have?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Well, we can see here that this is a document of the security administration which requests that information be collected about persons from the Yugoslav Peoples' Army who were taken prisoner. And the second part says that information should be sent about imprisoned members of the MUP and the ZNG of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was this sent to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: This was sent by the security administration and it was sent to the Chief of Security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary, and the Chief of Security sent it to me, along with his own accompanying letter, because what started happening was that many prisoners were taken, many prisoners -- rather, many soldiers from the Guards Brigade went missing and we needed to have clear records as to where people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this into evidence, Your Honours? Can we tender this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 818, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is marked as 65 ter -- as a 65 ter document, 3D 02, and in the system it is 3D 05-0003. It is a handwritten document and Mr. Sljivancanin is going to explain this to us, what this is. This is a report of the security organ of the 12th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, what is this? Can you describe it to us in terms of -- not in terms of content but in terms of form. What do we have in front of us now?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: This is one of the reports security organs of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and you will see, since the Operations Group was referred to several times here, never, ever did I receive either oral or written orders that I was Chief of Security of an Operations Group. I knew that I was Chief of Security of the Guards Brigade. And I'm not trying to say that anybody is lying, but here are my reports, here are the documents, so none of this was made up. In that report, I say what my counter-intelligence assessment is and what my knowledge is in the units of the Guards Brigade and in its zone, in terms of what my desk officers had learned by then and what I had learned by then, and I'm sending this to the Chief of Security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary. This is one of the reports. It is for the 11th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who wrote this document? Whose handwriting is this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Of my assistant for counter-intelligence, Major Mladen Karan, or rather, then captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Lest there be any misunderstanding, it says that the report is for the 11th, whereas we see here in the document itself that it's the 12th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I'll explain that, too. We sent it on the 12th of October, at 900 hours, depending on when the courier and when the post went. It was for the date of the 11th of October, but this is when we sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what do you know in terms of what happened to this report afterwards? Where was it sent to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: As it can be seen here, this report went to the Chief of Security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary. He gathered information there, and probably on other sides, too. Well, I don't know what his methods of work were; I'm not familiar with that. And on that basis, he wrote a brief, a piece of information, that he sent to the security administration. On the basis of information received from us, he would write his own information to the security administration, stating what the counter-intelligence situation was in the zone of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As we're going to see in the documents further on, did it ever happen that these documents would be retyped?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: It would happen that the Chief of Security, because we did not have the necessary resources on the ground, we would send all our reports written in hand and then sometimes he would attach them to his own document -- these documents of ours, as they were, attached to his report to the security administration, whereas sometimes our reports would be retyped and, as such, sent to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on this document because there is this retyped information on the basis of this handwritten information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like to ask that that be tendered, Your Honours. And we are going to analyse the content of the report later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 819, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document that I would like us to analyse is a document that is marked 3D 05-0018, and that is information dated the 13th of October. If we can please see it on the electronic system. 3D 05-- or rather, 03 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you now, Mr. Sljivancanin, what is this that we see on the screen now? What is it that we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: Here, on the screen, we see the form of information compiled by security organs in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, specifically this has to do with the Chief of Security of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary. This was compiled on the 13th of October, 1991, in three copies. Two were submitted to the security administration and one remained in the archives of the security organs of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary. The Chief of Security compiled this information concerning intelligence regarding the state of security in units and in the area of responsibility of the Guards Motorised Brigade on the basis of preceding information that I had sent on the 12th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to ask that we look at page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting my friend this morning. Can he please just refer us to the exact page in his bundle. We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I gave it to the interpreters and now I do not have the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first page is 23 in the English version so it is probably -- the first page is marked 23 and this is on page 3, so it's probably 26. The paragraph starts with about registering cases of looting in war. I will read that part very slowly though so then we will all be quite aware of what it is that I'm trying to ask the witness. Could we please have the page lifted a bit on the screen, on the e-court system because I'm going to read out the second paragraph, and that's how it's going to be easier for the interpreters as well who will be doing the sight translation. Thank you. "The work of security organs registered and documented several cases of war looting in the territory in the zone of combat actions by the Guards Motorised Brigade on -- this was committed by volunteers and members of the staff of TO Negoslavci. The mentioned crimes are assuming special proportions due to the fact that they are being carried out when combat action is taking place and combat positions are being abandoned and attack powers being weakened therefore. Operations information indicates that the looting is being carried out in the organisation of Milan Bibic, the commander of the staff of TO Negoslavci as well as his associate, Jovica Kresovic. In cooperation with the command organs, energetic measures are being taken to suppress the above-mentioned occurrences. "According to statements made by local persons, inter alia the parents of Popovic Banislav from the 1st Battalion of the military police, Boro Bugunovic, minister of the interior of the SAO -- SBIZS, Slavonia Barinja and Western Srem, was selling arms received to local persons at prices that ranged from 800 to 1800 Deutschemark, as well as food that came in as aid to the endangered population. According to some indications, part of the weapons that are owned by the JNA is even at this time in the basement of the Bugunovic house and it is being sold in cooperation with Bibic who is giving local persons special permits."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: I talked about this person a great deal and now we see other persons referred to here. Right now, I cannot remember their names but I remember this minister very well. All the time throughout our stay in this zone, we tried to establish law and order and to take all measures to prevent looting and any other type of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: This can be seen on the basis of our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next page. Next page, page 4 of B/C/S -- of the B/C/S version. Paragraph 2, will you please put that up. "According to information obtained by the security organ of the Guards Brigade, Muharem Besic, Captain first class, Chief of Security of the 453rd Motorised Brigade, while staying in the Negoslavci area with members of the reserve forces of the military police, unlawfully issued to civilians special permits in the attachment, thereby preventing any misuse. The members of the military police authorise in this way cruelly mistreated citizens and even carried out assassinations based on their own decisions. It was in this way that the messenger of the commander of the Croatian armed forces in Vukovar was killed, although it was well known who this person was and this made any further gathering of important intelligence impossible." Mr. Sljivancanin, can you tell us anything about this and what was your personal assignment in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: This was recorded at the time and it says that - and this was true - security organs have no -- how should I put it, power to protect anyone, not even one of their own. Each man fends for himself. What we recorded here reflects what we learned at the time. This unit in which this Chief of Security was, this gentleman, left our area as soon as the 4th or 5th of October. We forwarded information that we had to those in charge who were to continue processing this intelligence and gathering more intelligence as well as to make an assessment as to whether these were mere rumours or whether there was any substance to these stories. Our job was to forward this report, and then the higher levels of intelligence were supposed to verify this information and to collate it if necessary. Sometimes you can have information that is reliable. When intelligence work is being carried out based on that, it is our job to stop this work being carried out and to report any suspicions of falseness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think at this point, we deserve a rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Right. Could I just clarify one or two small matters just to assist me. I may be in error. Is my learned friend saying that -- as far as I can understand it, that Mr. Sljivancanin is saying that he was -- is he believed it to be, only the security organ for the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade as opposed to OG South? Because that is my understanding. And if that is the case, I've not seen that in my 65 ter summary. I've not seen it in any of the supplementary notes. I have not been aware of it being put to any of the witnesses. There are three or four witnesses, certainly I would have thought it should have been put to. But if I am in error, then I apologise. But could he possibly clarify that, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My understanding is that of yours, Mr. Moore. Is it correct, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like that to be the first question I ask Mr. Sljivancanin tomorrow: What is his personal view of OG South? That is one thing. The other thing is, while cross-examining witness Vukosavljevic, I put our case to him in no uncertain terms; namely, that Sljivancanin, or rather, the Chief of Security of the Guards Brigade, and I was using the expression "OG South," whereas Mr. Sljivancanin is adamant we should keep saying the "Guards Brigade," and tomorrow I'm about to explain that, or rather, he's about to explain that to us, that he was not in charge. And that was the sort of question that the witness Vukosavljevic was being asked. So the relationship between Operations Group South and the security organ is something that we have, so far, put to all of our witnesses in no uncertain terms. Mr. Sljivancanin has a view on Operations Group South. It's his own view. I was going to be asking that as the very first question tomorrow morning, because that may require a minute or two for his answer to be given, and then you will be familiar with his position on this very issue. He was a member of the command of OG South. You will hear more about that, too. However, he believes that he was not the Chief of Security of OG South. That's his position. He'll explain it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears, Mr. Moore, we must wait in patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask something, for this last document to be admitted, Your Honours, because we didn't enter it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I be clear how you describe this document? It's dated the 13th of October, as I understand it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document, dated the 13th of October, it contains a report dated the 12th of October, which you had previously seen. It's the handwritten report. If you look at the English, you will see both documents right there. They're very similar. I just wanted to give you the technical background of how exactly these reports are sent. I will call it the information dated the 13th of October by the Chief of Security of the cabinet for the Federal Secretary for All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 820, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will now adjourn until tomorrow, at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 25
